title: Hello, World
summary: Write to the console, and learn how a C# program is read.

steps.title: Your first program
body: A C# program is a list of **statements**. The computer runs them one at a time, top to bottom.
Read it from the inside out:
- `"Hello, World!"` is a **string**: text, wrapped in double quotes.
- `Console.WriteLine(...)` is a **method call**. `Console` is the terminal window, `WriteLine` writes one line to it.
- `;` ends the statement. Forgetting it is the most common first error.
In this track you build **Sidekick**, a developer assistant you run in your own terminal: `sk` greets you,
keeps your tasks and timers, writes your standup and charts your week. Every lesson adds one real piece of it,
written by you. The very first piece is its banner, and you write it in the next exercise.

steps.prompt: Which line prints `Hi` to the console?
steps.explain: The others each break one rule: wrong capitalisation, missing quotes around the text, and a missing `;`.

steps.title: Sidekick's banner
prompt: **Your first Sidekick piece.** Every time you type `sk`, this banner greets you. Print it exactly, four lines:
|   S I D E K I C K                  v0.1   |
Copy the characters carefully: one `WriteLine` per line, the text inside double quotes. Spaces count.
starter: // One Console.WriteLine per line of the banner
solution: Console.WriteLine("|   S I D E K I C K                  v0.1   |");

tests.name: Prints the four banner lines
expect: |   S I D E K I C K                  v0.1   |

hints: Four lines means four `Console.WriteLine("...");` statements, top to bottom.
The first and last lines are the same border. Copy the middle lines from the prompt, spaces included.
steps.explain: This exact code is now `Cli/Banner.cs` in your Sidekick. Open **Builds** to see it waiting for the next pieces.

steps.title: WriteLine and Write
body: `WriteLine` moves to a new line after printing. `Write` does not.
Anything after `//` is a **comment**: a note for humans that the compiler ignores.

steps.explain: `Write` keeps the cursor on the same line, so `1` and `2` join up. The third line is a comment and never runs.

steps.title: A status line from pieces
prompt: Sidekick often builds one line out of several parts. Use **three** `Console.Write` calls and one `Console.WriteLine`
so the program prints exactly these two lines:
Write `[ok] `, then `build passed`, then ` in 12s` with `Write`, and finish the line before printing `Done.`
hints: `Console.Write` keeps the cursor on the same line, so three of them build one line.
`Console.WriteLine()` with nothing inside just ends the line. Then print `Done.`

steps.prompt: Drag the lines into an order that prints `Ready`, `Set`, `Go!` on three separate lines.
steps.explain: Statements run top to bottom, in exactly the order you write them.

steps.title: Fix the tagline
prompt: Under the banner, Sidekick prints its tagline. This code should print exactly:
Tasks, timers and standups, right in your terminal.
It has **three** mistakes. Run it, read the errors, and fix them. This becomes `Cli/Tagline.cs` in your Sidekick.
starter: Console.WriteLine("Tasks, timers and standups, right in your terminal.")
solution: Console.WriteLine("Tasks, timers and standups, right in your terminal.");

expect: Tasks, timers and standups, right in your terminal.

hints: Line 1 is missing something at the very end.
Line 3 prints something the task never asked for, and `Done` has no quotes. The simplest fix is to delete the line.
